## Criterion 1 - the cause

`pumpAndSettle` exits only on a frame where nothing further is scheduled
(`flutter_test/lib/src/widget_tester.dart:715-721`):

```dart
do {
  if (binding.clock.now().isAfter(endTime)) {
    throw FlutterError('pumpAndSettle timed out');
  }
  await binding.pump(duration, phase);
  count += 1;
} while (binding.hasScheduledFrame);
```

`PatrolBinding extends LiveTestWidgetsFlutterBinding`
(`patrol-3.20.0/lib/src/binding.dart:43`), and that binding's `handleDrawFrame`
ends (`flutter_test/lib/src/binding.dart:2817-2825`):

```dart
if (_expectingFrame) {
  ...
  _expectingFrame = false;
} else if (framePolicy != LiveTestWidgetsFlutterBindingFramePolicy.benchmark) {
  platformDispatcher.scheduleFrame();
}
```

**`binding.dart:2823-2824` is the answer.** That `else` runs for every frame the
test did not itself pump. On a device vsync delivers those continuously, so each
schedules the next: a frame is always pending, `hasScheduledFrame` is never
false, the loop never exits.

Changing the frame policy cannot help. The branch excludes exactly one policy,
`benchmark`, and `pumpAndSettle` refuses to run under that one
(`widget_tester.dart:699-711`: *"hasScheduledFrame is never set to true ...
pumpAndSettle() cannot be used"*). Either frames are always scheduled or never.

**The app is not involved.** No frame callback, `SchedulerBinding`, `Ticker`,

one-shot in `core/utils/debouncer.dart:38`. `performance_screen_mixin.dart` - a

## The rule, and what it deliberately does not catch

Redaction is by **key name only, never by value shape**. Shape matching (a
JWT-looking regex) catches tokens under unexpected keys, but it also redacts
legitimate base64 payloads, hashes and opaque ids, and makes the redaction set
impossible to predict by reading the code.

Keys normalize to lowercase alphanumerics (`access_token`, `accessToken`,
`X-Access-Token` -> `accesstoken`), then match as a **fragment** (`password`,
`token`, `secret`, `apikey`, `credential`, `authorization`, `privatekey`,
`creditcard`, `cardnumber`, `signature`, ...) or **exactly** for names too short
to be safe fragments (`pin`, `otp`, `cvv`, `cvc`, `session`) - `pin` occurs
inside `shipping`. Bodies are an allow-list of walkable shapes: a `String`
decoding to a JSON object or array is walked field by field; form-encoded, plain
text, a bare JSON scalar (`jsonEncode('<token>')` parses cleanly), `FormData`
and streams are redacted wholesale.

The residual is pinned by two tests rather than left implicit: a JWT under the
key `blob` is still logged, and an OAuth `code` query parameter is not redacted
(`code` is also one of the most common non-secret field names there is).
`docs/api/core/network.md` names both.

### What changed

`ApiClient._createDio` now hands the `CacheInterceptor` it builds to the auth
interceptor via `attachResponseCache()`, mirroring the existing
`attachTransport()`. `_logoutUser()` clears it as a third independently
guarded, best-effort step. A null key-value store no longer `return`s early out
of the teardown - it used to, which would have skipped the new step whenever
nobody wired a key-value store.

### How criterion 3 was made genuinely comparative

Not two separate assertions. The test builds **two worlds from the same seeding
function** (one anonymous cached response, an access token, a refresh token, a
cached user blob), asserts `forced.state == explicit.state` **before** either
logout runs so the starting points are proven identical rather than assumed,
runs explicit `AuthRepositoryImpl.logout()` in one and drives a real 401 through
the assembled `ApiClient` in the other, then compares one snapshot map against
the other in a single `expect(forced.state, equals(explicit.state))`. The
snapshot is `{keyValueStore, accessToken, refreshToken}`, so any key either path
leaves behind is a diff. Two anti-vacuity guards follow: the end state must
differ from the seed, and it must be the fully torn-down state.

Cache *timestamp values* are normalised to a placeholder, because two worlds
seeded microseconds apart write different `DateTime.now()` strings; the
timestamp **keys** are still compared, so an entry one path removes and the
other keeps still fails.

### Retry policy decision

Chose the **container-level opt-out** over making startup failures `Error`s
(a lie in the type system to manipulate a framework heuristic) and over a
per-provider `retry:` (protects only providers someone remembered to annotate).
The hazard is the shape `await container.read(x.future)` with no listener,
which is every line of the startup sequence including ones not written yet.

Stated plainly: that container is also the app's runtime container, so Riverpod
auto-retry is now off app-wide. A container `Retry` is `(int, Object) ->
Duration?` and cannot see which provider failed, so "off for startup, default
elsewhere" is not expressible. Accepted because `RetryInterceptor` already
retries transient network failures one layer down with a visible, per-request
policy; Riverpod's retry reports as `AsyncLoading(retrying: true)`, which hides
error UIs behind up to ten invisible attempts; and nothing in `lib/` relied on
it - full suite green.

Retry is not gone, it is user-driven: `StartupFailureApp.onRetry` still calls
`main()`. Bounded (one attempt per tap), visible, and from a fresh container -
unlike an automatic retry of a half-finished migration. No wall-clock timeout
was added: with retry off the failure surfaces immediately, and a timeout would
add a worse failure mode (aborting a slow migration, then offering a button
that starts a second one over the same data).

Also covered beyond the path the issue names: the downgrade refusal
(`StorageDowngradeException`) and the stamp-write failure both added by #60, and
the guard in `main()` now spans the whole pre-first-frame sequence rather than
the migration alone.

### Criterion 3 - the one deviation, and it is #51's guard

The criterion names the stack `/` -> `/login` -> `/register`. **That stack
cannot exist in this app.** Unauthenticated, `/` redirects to `/login` before
it renders, so the bottom entry is never `/`. Authenticated, pushing `/login`
is redirected back to `/`, so the middle entry is never `/login`. Both are
#51's guard doing its job.

The guard was **not** weakened to make the literal wording testable. Three deep
is the minimum that tells a correct `popUntilRoute` apart from one that pops
until it cannot - at two deep both land in the same place - so the test asserts
the reachable three-deep equivalent `/login` -> `/register` -> `/login`,
popping to `/register` and checking `canPop()` is still true, and
`tasks_routes_test.dart` adds the authenticated `/` -> `/tasks` -> `/tasks/:id`
case. `criterion-3-REGRESSION-DEMO.log` runs that test against a copy of the
tree with the pre-fix body restored: it fails on `Expected: '/register' Actual:
'/login'`. The old assertion-free test at `navigation_extensions_test.dart:289`
passed against that same code.

## Criterion 2 - the one real judgement call, please read

I did not skip this. I measured it in both directions and then deliberately did
not ship half of it.

- **The bug is real.** With the entitlements as they were, a probe driving
  `FlutterSecureStorage.write` under `flutter test -d macos` fails with
  `PlatformException(..., Code: -34018, A required entitlement isn't present.)`.
  `SecureStorageService` swallows that, so tokens silently never persist.
- **The obvious fix has a cost I was not willing to take unilaterally.** With
  `keychain-access-groups` present - even as the *empty* array
  flutter_secure_storage's own macOS instructions give - `flutter build macos`
  **and** `flutter run -d macos` fail on any machine with no Apple development
  certificate:
  `error: "Runner" has entitlements that require signing with a development
  certificate.` (`security find-identity -v -p codesigning` here: `0 valid
  identities found`.)

For a starter template, turning that on by default makes a signing certificate a
prerequisite for building at all, including for the documented local run target.
So it ships **commented out in both macOS entitlements files**, with the
measurement written beside it, and the iOS half - which does **not** have this
problem - ships enabled and wired:
`ios/Runner/Runner.entitlements` plus `CODE_SIGN_ENTITLEMENTS` in all three
Runner configurations, confirmed by `flutter build ios --no-codesign` succeeding
(that is what `build.yml` runs).

quit, relaunch.

RFC 6531 (SMTPUTF8), at a domain of two or more RFC 1035 LDH labels, inside the
RFC 5321 size limits** (local part 64 octets, address 254, label 63).

Deliberately rejected, and why: quoted-string local parts, domain literals
(`user@[192.168.0.1]`), comments, single-label domains (`user@localhost`), and a
trailing root dot. RFC 5322 permits all of them; none is deliverable through the
public mail system from a sign-up form.

Deliberately **accepted**, because over-strictness is a real bug too: SMTPUTF8
local parts and U-label domains, punycode TLDs like `xn--p1ai` (an
alphabetic-only TLD rule would have rejected it), every printable ASCII `atext`
character, leading and trailing underscores, and digit-leading local parts and
domain labels. The reasoning is in the `Validators` class doc so the next person
does not have to re-derive it.

## Stored data: no migration implied

`DateFormatter` has **zero call sites** in `lib/` (`criterion-11-12-call-sites.log`),
so nothing was ever persisted through its lenient parse and the strict-parse
change cannot shift or reject stored data. The existing

before. The #60 migration framework is not needed.

What the survey did turn up is a genuine offset-less timestamp in

## Non-idempotent operations through the perf mixin

Nothing flows through the mixins today - `measureRepositoryOperation`,
`measureUseCaseOperation` and `measureDataSave` have zero call sites
(`criterion-11-12-call-sites.log`). But `measureDataSave` is *by design* the
write-path convenience method, and the mixin's own doc example wraps repository
writes, so the API exists to have non-idempotent work flow through it. The
duplicate execution was live the moment anyone used it as documented.

The fix is deliberately **stronger** than the #88 `RetryInterceptor` precedent,
not a weaker copy of it. #88 could classify the operation - RFC 9110 safe
methods replay, everything else replays only on `connectionTimeout`, with a
per-request opt-in defaulting off. The mixin receives an opaque
`Future<Result<T>> Function()`: there is no method, no headers, nothing to
classify, so no safe-method rule is even expressible. And a caller who wants
retry can wrap the call themselves - a *performance* mixin silently retrying is
the wrong place for that policy regardless. So: never re-run, and let an
instrumentation failure propagate instead of being papered over.

## Decisions, and what they cost

**Scan directories rather than refuse them.** Refusing a directory declaration
would mean deleting `assets/images/` and `assets/config/` from a starter
template whose point is to hand those directories to the user - the guard would
be rejecting the repository's own intended layout, and would be removed rather
than obeyed. The cost is stated in the tool header, in `pubspec.yaml` and in
`docs/guides/configuration.md`: **the walk sees the tree at the moment it
runs**, so a file added afterwards ships until something runs the check again.

**Match rule, by file name only.** Env files (`.env`, `.env.*` except
`.env.example`); private key and code-signing extensions (`.pem` `.key` `.p12`
`.pfx` `.p8` `.jks` `.keystore` `.mobileprovision` `.provisionprofile` - the
code-signing block of `.gitignore` minus the public certificate formats, plus
`.pem`/`.key`); and a short list of credential names (`secrets.{json,yaml,yml}`,
`credentials.json`, `service-account.json`, `service_account.json`,
`key.properties`, `google-services.json`, `GoogleService-Info.plist`).
Deliberately **not** matched: `.cer` / `.crt` / `.der`, because a certificate is
public by design and an SSL-pinning setup may legitimately ship one; and
ordinary configuration such as `config.json` or `app_config.yaml`, because a
rule that fires inside a directory literally named `assets/config/` would be
wrong on its first run and would get the whole guard switched off. The accepted
cost: a secret inside an innocuously named file is not detected.

**A directory acknowledgement must name the file.** A file inside a directory
has no line of its own, so the marker goes on the directory entry -
`- assets/config/ # env-asset-ack: .env.web, publishable values only` - and
covers only the file it names. A blanket directory ack would have been a
permanent off-switch, which is the opposite of what the inline marker is for.

## Mechanism

`paths-ignore` removed from `ci.yml`; the filter moved into the job as a
`Decide the gate scope` step that diffs `base...head` (or `before..after` on a
push) and drives `if:` on Setup Flutter, pub get, format, analyze and test.
One job, one check context, one copy of the path list, no third-party action.

Rejected:

- **`dorny/paths-filter` plus a same-named dummy job** - adds a third-party
  action to a repository that risk-gates dependency changes, and emits two
  check runs sharing the name `Quality gate`, which branch protection cannot
  tell apart.
- **A separate `ci-skip.yml` shim** - splits one gate's path list across two
  files that must be kept in sync by hand.
- **Changing nothing and requiring an existing always-reporting check instead.**
  The issue brief asked whether one of the four workflows already gives branch
  protection something adequate. It does not. **Issue refs** checks commit
  messages, not code. No **Strip** variant runs `dart format`, and all three
  analyze and test a *stripped* tree rather than the shipped one - PR #155
  proves it directly: the misformatted file turned Quality gate red while all
  three Strip jobs stayed green.

One deliberate tightening: the skip set is **narrower** than the old
`paths-ignore`. `.dart` is never inert, wherever it lives. `analysis_options.yaml`
does not exclude `docs/`, so `docs/verification/issue-48/aot_probe.dart` is
analyzed like any other source; the old filter would have let a broken evidence
probe through the gate and reddened `main` on an unrelated PR later.
Unresolvable diff ranges (`workflow_dispatch`, new branch, force push that
dropped `before`) fail **safe** and run the full gate.

## What a green Quality gate on a docs-only PR means

Not that format, analyze and test passed - that they **did not run**, because no
changed path can affect them. The job summary says which of the two happened and
lists every changed path, so the distinction is visible without reading the YAML.
A reviewer should read it as "nothing this gate guards could have changed",
never as "the code is green".

## The fix

`_CountingAuthInterceptor` replaces both sleeps with a happens-before. It
subclasses `AuthInterceptor`, counts entries into `onError`, and completes a
marker after `super.onError` returns - which is rigorous rather than
approximate, because `super.onError` reaches the guard and parks the request
*synchronously*. `await interceptor.seen(3)` therefore means "the guard has
processed all three 401s". Both tests then assert `refreshCalls == 1` **while
the refresh is still held open**, which is the single-flight property itself
rather than a downstream consequence of it.

### What marks a session dead

A monotonic counter, `SessionGeneration`
([`lib/core/session/session_generation.dart`](https://github.com/koniz-dev/flutter-starter/blob/main/lib/core/session/session_generation.dart)),
shared by `AuthInterceptor` and `AuthRepositoryImpl` through
`sessionGenerationProvider`. Read `current` before the round trip, check
`isCurrent(...)` immediately before persisting. `invalidate()` is called
synchronously, ahead of that method's own `await`s, by `logout()`, `login()`,
`register()` and `AuthInterceptor._logoutUser()`.

Not a `_terminated` flag, because a boolean answers "is there a session right
now" - the wrong question. Signing back in while an old refresh is open clears
the flag and the stale response lands on the **new** user's tokens. A
generation left behind can never become current again. Because `login()` and
`register()` invalidate too, a sign-in *not* preceded by a logout is covered as
well.

The same case dictates that a stale refresh **skips** its writes rather than
clearing the store: a compensating delete would destroy the tokens of a session
that started during the refresh. Covered by `a login completing during an old
refresh keeps the new session: the stale refresh skips its writes rather than
undoing them` (counterfactual: `Expected: 'session-2-access' / Actual:
'NEW-access-1'`).

`setAccessToken` is guarded in the interceptor; `cacheToken` and

`auth_repository_impl.dart` was unavoidable - two of the three writes live
there and criterion 1 names them - so the change there is one optional
constructor parameter, one field, three `invalidate()` lines and one check. No

## What the fix decided

**Grammar.** The ack payload is parsed, not searched:

```
ack       := 'env-asset-ack:' names? separator? prose?
names     := name (',' name)*
name      := a bare file name containing a dot - no spaces, no directory part
separator := ';' | an em or en dash | a hyphen with spaces around it
             | the first ',' segment that is not a name
```

The covered set is the leading comma-separated run of bare file names, each
compared to the file's own name exactly and case-insensitively. Comma is the
separator because the documented form already used one and changing it would
invalidate every ack an adopter has written; the ambiguity that creates is
settled by the shape of a segment, not its position - a segment with a space in
it is prose, which is what keeps `.env.web, publishable values only` working.
`;` and the dashes exist so `# env-asset-ack: .env.web - publishable values
only` parses with no comma at all. Requiring a dot in a name costs nothing
(every file the guard can flag has one) and buys the reading that a one-word
segment such as `reviewed` is prose rather than a file that will never exist.

**A stale ack** - a name matching no file in the directory - is a
`check_env_assets: note:` on stderr and does **not** change the exit code.
Hard-failing was the other candidate and was rejected: `.env` and `.env.*.local`
are gitignored and a web deployment may write its env file at deploy time, so a
fresh checkout can legitimately lack the file, and a red build there would
punish a tree that is strictly safer than the one the ack was written against. A
stale name cannot hide anything either - the file it names is absent, and any
file that is present is matched exactly or reported.

**The passing channel** stays, moved to stderr along with the acknowledged-file
reminder. That is not the blind spot this issue describes: the blind spot was
that the *load-bearing* signal lived there, a bundled unreviewed secrets file
producing one line and exit 0. That case now exits 1. What is left is advisory
about files a human has already signed off on, and acks that cover nothing.
